explanations: Standard and Datacenter share the same role set, RAM ceiling, and GUI options. The licensing difference is the virtualization rights: Standard grants two Windows Server Operating System Environments (OSEs) per fully-licensed host, while Datacenter grants unlimited OSEs. This is why Datacenter is the only economically rational choice for Hyper-V hosts running more than two VMs.

Server Core ships without the Server Graphics Shell, Windows Explorer, Internet Explorer, and most desktop binaries. The result is a roughly half-the-disk footprint compared to Desktop Experience and a meaningfully reduced attack surface (fewer running services, fewer patches to apply). Server Core is now the default installation option in the Windows Server installation wizard since Windows Server 2016.

Per the published Windows Server 2022 system requirements, the minimum RAM is 512 MB (2 GB for the Desktop Experience installation option). Note: minimum is the floor that lets Setup succeed; recommended values for production workloads are dramatically higher. The exam tests the published minimum specifically.

Server Manager (ServerManager.exe) is the bundled management console on Windows Server Desktop Experience and starts automatically when an administrator signs in. It surfaces role and feature installation, server group management, and links into the various MMC tools. The autostart behavior is configurable from Manage > Server Manager Properties.

Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security is a core layered-defense control. The Microsoft-documented operations practice is to ALLOW required traffic through targeted rules (per-profile and per-port) and to leave the firewall enabled. Disabling the firewall is a security regression and is not part of any first-day-of-install runbook. The other three (rename, static IP, patch) are all part of standard post-install hardening.

Get-WindowsFeature is part of the ServerManager module and returns a list of all features and roles with their install state (Installed / Available / Removed). It is the canonical inventory cmdlet on Windows Server for role/feature discovery and is the basis for Install-WindowsFeature and Uninstall-WindowsFeature.

New-NetIPAddress is the modern PowerShell cmdlet (from the NetTCPIP module, available on Windows Server 2012+) for assigning an IP address to an interface. The required parameters in this scenario are -InterfaceAlias (the friendly name of the NIC), -IPAddress (the address itself), and -PrefixLength (the subnet prefix in CIDR bits). Gateway is set separately via New-NetRoute or by adding -DefaultGateway.

Microsoft switched Windows Server licensing from per-processor to per-core starting with Windows Server 2016. Each physical server requires enough core licenses to cover all physical cores (minimum 16 cores per server, minimum 8 cores per physical processor), and each user or device accessing the server additionally requires a Windows Server CAL. WS2022 Standard and Datacenter retain this exact model.

GPT is the modern partition-table format that supersedes MBR. MBR is capped at 2 TB per disk and 4 primary partitions; GPT supports disks much larger than 2 TB (limited only by the OS) and up to 128 partitions per disk by default in Windows. UEFI firmware requires GPT for the boot disk; BIOS firmware can boot from either, though new installs default to GPT.

KMS is the on-premises activation service: an internal KMS host activates against Microsoft once, then activates client systems on the internal network for 180 days at a time (clients renew silently every 7 days). KMS is the standard activation path for air-gapped or restricted-internet networks. The alternative volume-activation path is Active Directory-Based Activation (ADBA), which uses the AD forest as the activation database; ADBA is also offline-capable.

The forest is the outermost boundary of an Active Directory deployment and is the true security boundary. All domains within a forest automatically trust each other (two-way transitive Kerberos trust), share a common schema and global catalog, and share a single configuration partition. An administrator with Enterprise Admin rights can operate across all domains in the forest. Two separate forests, by contrast, have no trust relationship by default and are genuinely isolated from each other.

Domain Local groups follow the AGDLP pattern's "DL" slot: they accept members from any domain in the forest (or even trusted external forests), but their permission assignments are restricted to resources within the same domain in which the group resides. This makes them the correct scope for assigning access to a specific server's share or printer — the resource lives in one domain, and the Domain Local group on that domain is granted access.

A single domain controller is a single point of failure for authentication, DNS, Group Policy application, and all AD-dependent services. Microsoft's guidance and industry best practice is a minimum of two domain controllers per domain so that if one fails (hardware failure, patching reboot, disaster), authentication and replication continue uninterrupted on the surviving DC. Three or more DCs are recommended for larger sites or when geographic distribution is involved, but two is the baseline minimum for any production environment.

Group Policy processes in LSDOU order: Local policy first, then Site-linked GPOs, then Domain-linked GPOs, then OU-linked GPOs (from the top-level OU down to the most deeply nested OU containing the object). Because later settings overwrite earlier settings when there is a conflict (and Block Inheritance / Enforce are not set), the OU-linked GPO applied last has the highest effective precedence — closest-to-the-object wins. The LSDOU acronym is the standard mnemonic and appears on the AZ-800 exam.

Add-ADGroupMember is the cmdlet from the ActiveDirectory module (RSAT) used to add one or more members to an Active Directory group. Example: Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "Domain Admins" -Members jsmith. The verb Add- is appropriate because the operation appends a member to an existing group — it does not replace the membership list.

The PDC (Primary Domain Controller) Emulator is the most operationally active FSMO role. It is responsible for: processing password changes replicated from other DCs in the domain immediately (rather than waiting on normal AD replication), handling account lockouts (lockout information from all DCs is sent to the PDC Emulator to provide a consistent lockout state), acting as the authoritative time source for the domain, and providing backward compatibility for legacy NTLM authentication. When a user's password is rejected at a DC, that DC queries the PDC Emulator before locking the account in case a recent password change has not yet replicated.

Active Directory Administrative Center (ADAC) was introduced in Windows Server 2008 R2 and is built on PowerShell. When you perform any action in the ADAC GUI (create a user, reset a password, enable the Recycle Bin), the tool displays the equivalent PowerShell commands in its "Windows PowerShell History" pane at the bottom of the window. This makes ADAC a teaching tool as well as an administrative tool — administrators can learn exact cmdlet syntax by performing GUI operations and reading the generated PowerShell.

AGDLP stands for Accounts → Global groups → Domain Local groups → Permissions. The pattern is: place user accounts into Global groups (scoped to the domain where accounts live), nest those Global groups into Domain Local groups (where the resource resides), and assign permissions to the Domain Local group. This design scales across a forest because Global groups aggregate users by function and Domain Local groups aggregate access by resource. In forests with multiple domains, Universal groups are inserted between Global and Domain Local, yielding AGUDLP.

Search-ADAccount -LockedOut is the correct cmdlet from the ActiveDirectory module. It queries Active Directory for all accounts that are currently locked out and returns the results. It can be combined with -UsersOnly to limit results to user accounts (excluding computer accounts). Example full usage: Search-ADAccount -LockedOut -UsersOnly | Select-Object Name, SamAccountName. The Search-ADAccount cmdlet has a family of similar switches: -Disabled, -PasswordExpired, -AccountInactive, etc.

The userPrincipalName (UPN) is the user's internet-style login name in the format username@domain.com (or any registered UPN suffix). It is used for modern authentication, including Azure AD / Entra ID hybrid scenarios, and is the login format prompted by Windows 10/11 sign-in screens. The UPN suffix does not have to match the AD domain name — organizations can add custom UPN suffixes (e.g., jsmith@contoso.com even if the AD domain is corp.contoso.local).

MBR (Master Boot Record) uses 32-bit Logical Block Addressing (LBA) fields to describe partitions. With 512-byte sectors, 2^32 sectors × 512 bytes = 2,199,023,255,552 bytes, which is approximately 2 TB (2 tebibytes). Any disk capacity beyond 2 TB is inaccessible to the operating system when using MBR — the space simply cannot be addressed. This is the fundamental technical reason GPT replaced MBR for large-capacity disks.

Initialize-Disk is the PowerShell cmdlet from the Storage module that writes a partition table (MBR or GPT) to a raw disk, making it ready for partitioning. The typical parameters are -Number (the disk number from Get-Disk) and -PartitionStyle (MBR or GPT). Example: Initialize-Disk -Number 1 -PartitionStyle GPT. After initialization, New-Partition and Format-Volume complete the setup.

UEFI firmware requires GPT (GUID Partition Table) for the boot disk. The UEFI specification defines the EFI System Partition (ESP) as a GPT partition type; MBR disks lack the partition type GUID required for the ESP. While UEFI systems can read MBR data disks, only GPT can be the boot disk on a UEFI system. GPT also provides benefits beyond UEFI compatibility: support for disks larger than 2 TB, up to 128 partitions, and redundant partition table headers at both ends of the disk.

Storage Spaces two-way mirroring (the standard Mirror resiliency type) requires a minimum of 2 physical disks. Each write is duplicated to both disks, providing fault tolerance for a single disk failure. Three-way mirroring, which can survive two simultaneous disk failures, requires a minimum of 5 disks. Simple (no resiliency) requires 1 disk. Parity (single-parity equivalent to RAID 5) requires a minimum of 3 disks.

New-SmbShare is the PowerShell cmdlet from the SmbShare module used to create a new SMB (Server Message Block) file share. Required parameters include -Name (the share name) and -Path (the local folder path to share). Optional parameters include -Description, -FullAccess, -ReadAccess, -ChangeAccess, and -NoAccess to set share-level permissions at creation time. Example: New-SmbShare -Name "Data" -Path "D:\Shares\Data" -FullAccess "CONTOSO\Domain Admins".

When a user accesses a resource over the network, Windows calculates effective access by intersecting NTFS permissions and share permissions: the most restrictive combination governs. For example, if the share grants Full Control but NTFS grants only Read, the effective permission is Read. Conversely, if NTFS grants Full Control but the share grants only Read, the effective permission is again Read. Neither permission set alone determines access — Windows applies the intersection (logical AND) of the two permission sets. Local access (sitting at the console) bypasses share permissions entirely and is governed solely by NTFS.

A dollar sign appended to a share name (e.g., Data$, C$) makes the share hidden — it will not appear when users browse the network or run net view \\servername. However, hidden shares are not access-protected by the $ symbol itself; someone who knows the full UNC path (\\server\Data$) can still connect if they have the appropriate share and NTFS permissions. Administrative shares such as C$, D$, ADMIN$, and IPC$ are created automatically by Windows and are hidden by default, but the $ convention can be applied to any share name the administrator creates.

Simple resiliency (no redundancy, equivalent to RAID 0) uses 100% of the pooled disk capacity for data storage. Because it writes no additional copies and no parity data, it is the most storage-efficient option. For example, three 1 TB drives in a Simple space yield ~3 TB of usable storage. The tradeoff is zero fault tolerance — any single disk failure results in data loss. Simple is appropriate only for scratch space, caches, or non-critical data where capacity is the priority.

The three-stage PowerShell pipeline for bringing a raw disk to a formatted, usable volume is: Initialize-Disk (writes the partition table) → New-Partition (creates a partition and assigns a drive letter) → Format-Volume (applies a file system such as NTFS or ReFS). In practice these are often combined with Get-Disk at the front to identify the target disk by number or property, and New-Partition is given the -AssignDriveLetter or -DriveLetter parameter. The pipeline works because Initialize-Disk passes the disk object downstream and New-Partition passes the partition object downstream.

NTFS (New Technology File System) is the standard file system for Windows Server data volumes. It provides: per-file and per-folder permission inheritance (ACLs), file encryption via EFS, compression, disk quotas, volume shadow copies (VSS), support for files larger than 4 GB, and volumes larger than 2 TB (with GPT). ReFS (Resilient File System) is an alternative for large-scale storage scenarios (Storage Spaces Direct) with better integrity checking, but NTFS remains the default and recommended choice for general-purpose server data volumes and for any volume that needs to be shared via SMB.

Hyper-V is a Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor. A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the physical hardware and manages the hardware resources itself, with the host operating system running as a privileged virtual machine (called the management partition or "parent partition" in Hyper-V terminology). Hyper-V's core component (hvix64.exe / hvax64.exe) loads before the Windows kernel and has direct hardware access. This architecture provides better performance and stronger isolation than Type 2 hypervisors.

Generation 2 virtual machines in Hyper-V support UEFI firmware, Secure Boot, and additional features such as PXE boot from a synthetic network adapter and SCSI-based boot (no IDE emulation). Generation 2 VMs use only synthetic devices (no emulated legacy hardware like a virtual IDE controller or floppy drive), which reduces attack surface and improves boot speed. Generation 2 is supported for Windows 8/Windows Server 2012 and later guest operating systems, and for 64-bit Linux guests.

An External virtual switch binds to a physical network adapter on the Hyper-V host and bridges virtual machine traffic onto the physical network. VMs connected to an External switch receive IP addresses from the physical network's DHCP server, can communicate with other physical hosts, and can reach external networks (including the internet) through the physical network's router — exactly as if each VM had its own physical NIC plugged into the physical switch.

New-VM is the PowerShell cmdlet from the Hyper-V module used to create a new virtual machine. Key parameters include -Name (the VM display name), -Generation (1 or 2), -MemoryStartupBytes (startup RAM), -NewVHDPath and -NewVHDSizeBytes (to create a new virtual hard disk), and -SwitchName (the virtual switch to connect to at creation). Example: New-VM -Name "WebServer01" -Generation 2 -MemoryStartupBytes 4GB -NewVHDPath "D:\VMs\WebServer01.vhdx" -NewVHDSizeBytes 60GB -SwitchName "External".

Production Checkpoints use the Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS) inside the guest operating system to create an application-consistent snapshot. Because VSS quiesces running applications (SQL Server, Exchange, etc.) before the snapshot, the resulting checkpoint contains a consistent state that can be safely restored without database corruption or transaction log inconsistency. This is equivalent to what enterprise backup agents do. Production Checkpoints are the default checkpoint type in Hyper-V on Windows Server 2016 and later.

The VHDX format (introduced with Windows Server 2012 as the successor to VHD) supports virtual hard disks up to 64 TB in size. The older VHD format was capped at 2 TB. The 64 TB ceiling of VHDX addresses the storage needs of large database VMs and makes VHDX viable for nearly all enterprise workloads that previously required pass-through physical disks. VHDX also includes journaling to protect against data corruption during host power failures.

An Internal virtual switch creates a virtual network segment that includes both VMs connected to the switch and the Hyper-V host management OS, but does not bridge to the physical network adapter. This is the correct switch type for scenarios where VMs need to communicate with the host (e.g., file transfers, management connections from the host) but should not have direct access to the physical LAN. The host can then optionally share its internet connection via Internet Connection Sharing or Windows NAT if outbound internet is needed.

Dynamic Memory is a Hyper-V feature that allows the hypervisor to dynamically adjust the RAM allocated to a running VM between a configured minimum and maximum value based on the VM's actual workload demand. When the VM's memory pressure decreases, Hyper-V reclaims RAM for use by other VMs; when pressure increases, it allocates more RAM (up to the configured maximum). Dynamic Memory is configured per-VM and requires Integration Services in the guest OS to communicate memory pressure signals to the hypervisor.

Hyper-V Replica replicates virtual machines from a primary host to a replica host (which can be at a remote disaster recovery site) using asynchronous replication. Changes are sent at configurable intervals (30 seconds, 5 minutes, or 15 minutes). Because it is asynchronous, there is a small replication lag — if the primary site fails, the replica may be slightly behind the primary's state. At the recovery site, administrators initiate a planned or unplanned failover to bring the replica VM online. Hyper-V Replica supports extended replication to a third site (Extend Replication).

Hyper-V requires CPU hardware virtualization extensions to be enabled in BIOS/UEFI before the role can be installed or before nested virtualization can function. Intel calls these extensions VT-x (Virtualization Technology for x86); AMD calls them AMD-V (AMD Virtualization). These extensions allow the hypervisor to intercept and handle privileged instructions from guest operating systems without emulation overhead. On many OEM systems these features are disabled by default in the UEFI firmware and must be enabled manually. The absence of enabled hardware virtualization extensions causes the Hyper-V role installation to fail with an error indicating the processor does not meet requirements.

The fundamental architectural distinction is that containers share the host operating system kernel rather than running a separate kernel for each instance. A container uses Linux kernel namespaces and cgroups (or Windows container isolation primitives) to create isolated process environments without the overhead of booting a full OS. This makes containers significantly lighter than VMs — they start in seconds rather than minutes and use a fraction of the RAM. The tradeoff is a weaker isolation boundary: all containers on a host share the same kernel, so a kernel vulnerability potentially affects all containers simultaneously.

Hyper-V isolation (also called Hyper-V containers) runs each container inside a lightweight, dedicated Hyper-V virtual machine with its own kernel instance. This provides a hardware-enforced security boundary equivalent to full VM isolation — a vulnerability that escapes the container namespace cannot cross the Hyper-V hypervisor boundary to affect other containers or the host. Hyper-V isolation is the required mode when running untrusted workloads or when the container OS kernel version does not match the host OS kernel version.

The Windows Nano Server container image is approximately 300 MB compressed (the uncompressed size varies by version but is typically in the 300–400 MB range). This is dramatically smaller than the Windows Server Core container image (~3–5 GB) and the full Windows Server image. The small footprint is by design: Nano Server as a container base image strips virtually all management tools, all GUI components, and most OS subsystems, leaving only the minimal runtime needed to host .NET applications and similar workloads. This size makes Nano Server attractive for microservices deployments where pull time and storage cost matter.

docker ps lists all currently running containers, showing their container ID, image, command, creation time, status, ports, and name. Adding the -a flag (docker ps -a) lists all containers regardless of state (running, exited, paused). The ps name derives from the Unix ps (process status) command, as containers are fundamentally OS processes in an isolated namespace. docker ps is one of the most commonly used Docker commands for container status inspection.

Starting with Windows Server 2019, Nano Server is available exclusively as a container base image. Microsoft removed the ability to deploy Nano Server as a standalone host operating system (on bare metal or as a VM). The decision was driven by the fact that Server Core with PowerShell provides most of what Nano Server offered as a host OS, and the complexity of managing a headless, PowerShell-remoting-only host at scale outweighed the size savings. As a container image, Nano Server retains its small footprint value for microservices and .NET application containers.

The FROM instruction is the first (and mandatory) instruction in a Dockerfile. It specifies the parent image from which the new image is built. Every Dockerfile must begin with a FROM instruction (or an ARG instruction that is then referenced by FROM). Example: FROM mcr.microsoft.com/windows/nanoserver:ltsc2022. All subsequent Dockerfile instructions (RUN, COPY, CMD, EXPOSE, etc.) operate on top of the layer stack established by the FROM image.

On Windows, the default networking driver for Docker containers is NAT (Network Address Translation), not Bridge as it is on Linux. Docker on Windows creates a virtual NAT network (nat by default) through which containers receive IP addresses in the 172.16.x.x or 172.17.x.x range and communicate with external networks via the host's IP address through NAT. This is a Windows-specific behavior — the nat driver is implemented using the Windows Container Network Interface (CNI) and Windows's built-in NAT capabilities. On Linux, Docker's default is the bridge driver.

A container image is a static, read-only, layered file system that contains the application code, runtime, libraries, and configuration needed to run an application. A container is the live, running instance created from that image. When Docker starts a container, it adds a thin writable layer on top of the image's read-only layers — this writable layer captures any changes made during the container's lifetime. When the container is stopped and deleted, the writable layer is discarded (unless explicitly committed to a new image). Multiple containers can run simultaneously from the same image, each with its own independent writable layer.

The -v flag (or --volume) in docker run mounts a Docker volume or a host directory into the container at a specified path. Data written to the mounted path is stored in the volume (managed by Docker) or on the host filesystem, both of which persist after the container is stopped or deleted. Example: docker run -v C:\data:C:\appdata myimage. Named volumes (docker volume create mydata) are the preferred Docker-native approach; bind mounts (-v C:\host\path:C:\container\path) are an alternative using host filesystem paths directly.

Process-isolated Windows containers share the host kernel directly. Because there is no abstraction layer between the container and the host kernel, the container's base image OS version must match the host OS version (or a compatible subset). For example, a Windows Server 2022 container image can run with process isolation only on a Windows Server 2022 host. If the versions do not match, the container engine will refuse to start the container in process-isolation mode. The solution for mismatched versions is to use Hyper-V isolation, which provides its own kernel instance and is version-flexible.

Windows Server Failover Clustering (WSFC) is designed to provide high availability for workloads such as SQL Server, Hyper-V VMs, file servers, and other services. When a cluster node fails (hardware failure, patch reboot, network loss), the cluster automatically moves the affected services (clustered roles) to a surviving node with minimal downtime. This automatic failover is the defining purpose of a failover cluster. High availability is measured by the reduction in unplanned downtime compared to a standalone server.

Quorum is the voting mechanism that determines which subset of cluster nodes has authority to keep the cluster running. In a split-brain scenario, a network partition causes cluster nodes to lose communication with each other; without quorum, both sides might believe they are the legitimate cluster and begin running services simultaneously, causing data corruption on shared resources. Quorum prevents this by requiring a majority of votes (from nodes and optionally a witness resource) before a partition is allowed to keep the cluster online. The partition without quorum-majority stops its cluster service and yields control.

Cloud Witness, introduced in Windows Server 2016, uses an Azure Blob Storage container as the quorum witness. It stores a small blob file in Azure that serves as the tiebreaker vote in quorum calculations. Cloud Witness is ideal for stretch clusters spanning multiple physical sites — rather than placing a witness disk or file share in one of the sites (which creates an implicit preference for that site in split-brain scenarios), the witness is in Azure and is geographically neutral. It requires an Azure Storage account and internet connectivity from all cluster nodes.

Cluster Shared Volumes (CSV) allow multiple cluster nodes to simultaneously read from and write to the same volume through a single coordinated namespace. Without CSV, a clustered disk can only be owned by one node at a time; other nodes must fail it over to access it. With CSV, all Hyper-V nodes in a cluster can read and write their respective VM virtual hard disks on the same volume concurrently, enabling features like live migration without the complexity of migrating disk ownership. CSV uses a metadata coordinator node but distributes I/O across all nodes.

Suspend-ClusterNode pauses a cluster node for maintenance operations such as patching or hardware servicing. When a node is suspended (paused), the cluster drain mechanism moves all clustered roles off the node to other nodes before the node enters maintenance mode. This prevents service interruption during planned maintenance. After maintenance is complete, Resume-ClusterNode brings the node back online and the cluster can rebalance roles back to it. This is the PowerShell equivalent of right-clicking a node in Failover Cluster Manager and selecting "Pause."

Live migration moves a running VM from one cluster node to another without any perceptible downtime — the VM's memory pages are iteratively copied to the destination node while the VM continues running, then a final brief cutover (typically milliseconds) switches execution to the destination. Quick migration is the older method: it saves the VM state to disk (similar to hibernation), moves the saved state to the destination node, and restores it there. Quick migration causes a brief service interruption (seconds to a minute depending on VM memory size) but requires less network bandwidth than live migration since it does not need to transfer memory pages live.

Cluster-Aware Updating (CAU) is a Windows Server feature that automates the process of installing Windows updates across all cluster nodes while maintaining service availability. CAU orchestrates the update process node by node: it drains roles from a node (using Suspend-ClusterNode), applies patches and reboots the node, resumes the node, then moves on to the next node. Because clustered roles remain running on the non-updating nodes throughout the process, CAU achieves near-zero downtime patching for cluster-hosted workloads. CAU can be run in self-updating mode (the cluster updates itself on a schedule) or remote-updating mode (triggered externally).

Test-Cluster runs the Cluster Validation tool against the specified servers. It performs a comprehensive suite of hardware, network, storage, and system configuration tests to verify that the servers meet the requirements for a supported failover cluster. Microsoft's support policy requires that Test-Cluster passes with no errors or warnings before a cluster configuration is supported. Running the validation tests before New-Cluster surfaces incompatibilities (mismatched NIC drivers, non-shared storage, network path errors) that would cause cluster failures in production.

Storage Spaces Direct (S2D) is a software-defined storage feature introduced in Windows Server 2016 Datacenter Edition. It aggregates the local direct-attached storage (NVMe, SSD, HDD) from multiple cluster nodes into a shared storage pool, eliminating the need for an external SAN or SAS fabric. S2D uses the SMB Direct (RDMA) network path between nodes for inter-node storage traffic. The resulting storage pool can be used to create CSV volumes for Hyper-V VMs, file shares, and other clustered workloads. S2D is the storage foundation of Azure Stack HCI.

A preferred owner is a node specified in a clustered role's properties that indicates the node the cluster should place that role on when the cluster is healthy and the role is available. If the preferred owner is online and meets requirements, the cluster moves the role back to it after a failover (during auto-failback, if configured) or starts it there when the cluster first comes online. Preferred owners are a placement preference, not a hard restriction — if the preferred owner is unavailable, the cluster can still run the role on any eligible node listed in the possible owners. This allows administrators to enforce an intended layout (e.g., even distribution of VM load) without locking out failover capability.

Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc) is the built-in MMC snap-in for reading the Windows event log subsystem. It surfaces the four main channels (System, Application, Security, Setup) plus Applications and Services Logs. Task Manager shows live process/performance data; Resource Monitor shows granular CPU/disk/network/memory usage in real time; Device Manager manages hardware drivers and devices — none of these display event log entries.

The Security event log records audit events generated by the Local Security Authority (LSA): successful and failed logons, privilege use, account management, object access, policy changes, and more. Audit policy settings (via Group Policy or auditpol) control which categories are written here. The System log records OS and driver events; the Application log records events from user-mode applications; the Setup log records installation activity — none are the home for logon/access auditing.

Get-WinEvent is the current preferred cmdlet for querying event logs. It supports the modern ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) log infrastructure, can query structured XML filters, reads .evtx log files directly, and handles both classic and modern log channels. Get-EventLog is the legacy cmdlet (works only on classic logs, deprecated for new scripts). Read-Event and Show-EventLog are not real PowerShell cmdlets.

Industry guidance for % Processor Time sustained over a monitoring interval is that values consistently above 80% indicate a CPU bottleneck requiring investigation (more cores, workload distribution, or process tuning). Values under 80% leave headroom for burst activity. "Less than 95%" and "less than 100%" are too permissive — a processor pegged at 90-99% leaves no headroom and will degrade response time under any additional load. "Less than 50%" is the steady-state ideal for a lightly loaded server but is not the standard alert threshold.

Avg. Disk Queue Length measures the average number of read and write requests that were queued for the disk during the sample interval. A sustained value above 2 per physical spindle (or above 1 for SSDs) signals that the disk cannot service requests as fast as they arrive — the definition of an I/O bottleneck. % Disk Time shows what fraction of time the disk is busy but can saturate and stop increasing before queue length does. Disk Bytes/sec measures throughput (not congestion). Current Disk Queue is an instantaneous snapshot (not an average) and is too noisy for trend analysis.

A Data Collector Set (DCS) in Performance Monitor (perfmon.exe) is a named container that groups together performance counters, event trace providers, and system configuration data, then collects them on a defined schedule and stores results in a log file. This is the mechanism used to capture baseline data, trend analysis, and capacity planning over time. It is not a backup tool, a network capture tool (that would be Wireshark/netsh trace/Network Monitor), or a log archive format.

Windows Admin Center is an agentless management gateway. It communicates with managed servers using existing Windows protocols: WinRM (Windows Remote Management) for PowerShell remoting, SMB for file operations, and RDP for remote desktop sessions. No additional agent software needs to be installed on the managed machines, which is a key architectural advantage over older agent-based management platforms. Network connectivity, WinRM, and PowerShell remoting are all prerequisites — only an installed agent is NOT required.

A memory leak in an application manifests as the process's Private Bytes counter (memory exclusively allocated to that process, not shared) growing monotonically over the lifetime of the process without any corresponding release. This pattern — steady growth over hours or days — is the diagnostic signature of a leak. Available MBytes dropping to zero immediately suggests a sudden large allocation, not a slow leak. Pages/sec spiking at launch is normal paging behavior. Cache Bytes being high is expected and healthy — Windows uses available RAM for the file system cache and releases it on demand; this is not a leak indicator.

Get-Counter (from the Microsoft.PowerShell.Diagnostics module) retrieves performance counter values in real time. It accepts counter paths in the standard \Object(Instance)\Counter format and supports continuous sampling at a specified interval via -Continuous and -SampleInterval. Get-Performance, Measure-Counter, and Read-Performance are not real PowerShell cmdlets.

Event ID 4624 "An account was successfully logged on" is written to the Security log for every successful interactive, network, or service logon. This is the first ID reviewed in logon auditing and forensics. 4625 is a failed logon attempt (wrong password or locked account). 4634 is an account logoff event. 4672 is "Special privileges assigned to new logon" — generated when an account with administrative or sensitive privileges logs on, often appearing alongside 4624 for admin accounts.

The DNS "A" (Address) record maps a fully qualified domain name to a 32-bit IPv4 address. It is the most fundamental record type and the primary record queried when a client resolves a hostname. CNAME (Canonical Name) creates an alias pointing to another hostname. MX (Mail Exchanger) identifies the mail servers for a domain. PTR (Pointer) performs the reverse — it maps an IP address back to a hostname in the .in-addr.arpa namespace.

PTR (Pointer) records live in reverse lookup zones (.in-addr.arpa for IPv4, .ip6.arpa for IPv6) and map an IP address to a hostname. Reverse lookups are used by tools like nslookup, ping -a, and by services that log or validate connecting IP addresses. A records do forward lookups (name to IP). CNAME creates hostname aliases. SRV records advertise service endpoints by name, port, and protocol.

When DNS zones are stored in Active Directory (AD-integrated zones), zone data is replicated through the AD replication topology, which is multi-master — any domain controller running DNS can accept and replicate zone updates. This contrasts with file-based secondary zones where only the primary zone master accepts writes. AD-integrated zones also support secure dynamic updates, which require NTLM or Kerberos authentication before a record is registered or modified, preventing unauthorized clients from polluting DNS. Query speed, CNAME support, and reverse lookup zones are available in both file-based and AD-integrated DNS.

Active Directory relies heavily on SRV (Service Location) records in DNS to publish the location of domain controllers and their services. The netlogon service on each DC automatically registers SRV records such as _ldap._tcp.<domain> and _kerberos._tcp.<domain> during startup. Client computers query these SRV records to discover which DCs are available, on which ports, and with what priority and weight (for load distribution). Without correct SRV records, AD authentication and replication fail. A records also exist for DCs but are used for direct name-to-IP resolution, not service discovery.

A DNS forwarder is a DNS server configured to send queries for domains it does not host to a designated upstream resolver, typically an ISP resolver or a public DNS service. This allows an internal DNS server to resolve external names (internet hostnames) without needing to perform full recursive resolution itself. Forwarders do not define zones, do not replicate AD data, and are distinct from the DNS cache (which stores already-resolved results locally as a byproduct of any resolution, not as a forwarder function).

AD-integrated zones use multi-master replication through Active Directory: every domain controller hosting the zone can accept dynamic DNS updates. In contrast, a traditional file-based primary zone has a single primary master that accepts updates; secondary zones are read-only copies that receive zone transfers from the primary; stub zones hold only NS records pointing to authoritative servers and do not accept updates at all. The multi-master update capability of AD-integrated zones is their defining advantage for environments with multiple DCs.

Reverse lookup zones use the .in-addr.arpa namespace with the octets of the network address written in reverse order (right-to-left). For a /24 subnet, the host octet is omitted — only the three network octets are used, reversed. For 192.168.1.0/24: reverse the three network octets (192 -> 168 -> 1 becomes 1 -> 168 -> 192), giving 1.168.192.in-addr.arpa. Option [0] omits the reversal. Option [2] includes the host octet (unnecessary for a /24 and incorrect zone naming). Option [3] reverses only two octets incorrectly.

Resolve-DnsName (from the DnsClient module) performs DNS lookups from a Windows client or server. It accepts a name or IP, supports specifying record type (-Type A, -Type MX, etc.) and the DNS server to query (-Server), and returns structured output. Get-DnsServerZone lists zones configured on a DNS server — it does not perform lookups. Test-Connection is the PowerShell equivalent of ping (ICMP or TCP) — it resolves names as a side effect but is not a DNS query tool. Get-DnsClientCache displays the local DNS resolver cache, not live query results.

DNS scavenging is an automated cleanup mechanism that removes stale dynamic resource records — records that were registered via dynamic DNS (DDNS) and have not been refreshed within the no-refresh interval plus the refresh interval (default: 7 + 7 = 14 days total). Stale records accumulate when computers are decommissioned, renamed, or moved without their DNS records being deleted. Scavenging does not remove duplicate records (there is no dedup engine), does not touch PTR records selectively or globally, and does not affect forwarder configuration (which is a server-level setting, not a zone record).

Secure dynamic updates (available only on AD-integrated zones) require the registering client to authenticate using NTLM or Kerberos. Only domain-joined computers and authenticated domain users can dynamically register or update records. This prevents rogue machines (unauthorized workstations, attackers) from injecting or overwriting DNS records — a common attack vector on networks using unsecured dynamic updates. The DNS server itself is the target of the updates, not the origin; only DCs can register is too restrictive (member servers and workstations also register their own A records via DDNS).

DORA is the standard four-step DHCP handshake: the client broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER, the server responds with a DHCPOFFER, the client broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST selecting the offer, and the server confirms with a DHCPACK.
Per RFC 2131, T1 (the first renewal attempt) occurs at 50% of the lease duration. T2 (the rebinding attempt, contacting any server) occurs at 87.5% (7/8).
A DHCP reservation ties a specific IP address to a client's MAC address so that client always receives the same IP from DHCP.
DHCP Option 3 specifies the Router (default gateway). Option 1 is the subnet mask. Option 6 is DNS servers. Option 15 is the domain name.

APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) triggers when a Windows client sends DHCPDISCOVER and receives no DHCPOFFER within the timeout window. The client self-assigns a 169.254.0.0/16 address. This is not caused by DHCP overload, lease expiry, or IP conflict detection (those generate different behaviors).
In Windows Server DHCP failover Hot Standby mode, the standby server reserves 5% of the address pool by default to service clients if it takes over as active. The active server handles 95%.

AD authorization (a domain-level check performed during DHCP service startup) prevents unauthorized DHCP servers from handing out leases on the network. An unauthorized server on a domain-joined network detects other authorized servers and shuts down. DNS integration, failover, and reservations do not require AD authorization.

The standard cmdlet for creating a new DHCP scope is Add-DhcpServerv4Scope (index 1). New-DhcpServerv4Scope (index 0) does not exist as a shipping cmdlet — the DhcpServer module uses Add- for creation. Set-DhcpServerv4Scope modifies an existing scope. Create-DhcpServerv4Scope is not a real cmdlet.

A superscope is an administrative grouping that allows a DHCP server to service clients from multiple IP subnets on the same physical network (multinetting). It is not used for server combination, failover, or lease configuration.

MCLT (Maximum Client Lead Time) is a DHCP failover parameter that defines the maximum period one server can extend a lease beyond what the partner server knows about, without confirmation. It is used during the partner-down state to prevent IP conflicts when the partner server eventually recovers.

explanations: LSDOU is the mnemonic for Group Policy Object (GPO) application order: Local policy is applied first (settings in the local computer's Group Policy editor), then Site-linked GPOs, then Domain-linked GPOs, then OU-linked GPOs (from parent OU to child OU). Because later-applied GPOs win (with the same precedence), OU-linked GPOs have the highest effective precedence, and local policy has the lowest. The other three options invent terms that do not exist in Group Policy documentation.

Each GPO has two components: the Group Policy Container (GPC), which is an object in the Active Directory database, and the Group Policy Template (GPT), which is a folder structure stored in SYSVOL and replicated to all domain controllers via DFS-R (or FRS on older domains). The GPT contains the actual policy files: Administrative Templates (.admx/.adml references), security settings, scripts, and software installation packages. The GPC in AD contains only metadata (version numbers, links). Storing GPT in SYSVOL enables file replication to all DCs and client access via UNC path \\domain\SYSVOL.

Block Inheritance is a flag on an OU (or site or domain) that prevents GPOs linked higher in the hierarchy (parent OUs, domain, site) from flowing down to that container. GPOs linked directly to the OU itself still apply. It is used when an OU needs an isolated policy environment (e.g., a DMZ or test environment). Block Inheritance does not delete GPOs, does not remove child OUs, and does not affect logon capability. Note: Block Inheritance can be overridden by GPOs with the Enforced (No Override) flag set at a higher level.

The Enforced flag (formerly called "No Override" in older Windows versions) is set on a GPO link. When a GPO link is Enforced, that GPO flows down through the hierarchy regardless of any Block Inheritance settings on child containers. This allows domain administrators to mandate settings that OUs cannot exempt themselves from. Security Filtering controls which security principals the GPO applies to. WMI Filtering applies or skips a GPO based on WMI query results about the target computer. Loopback Processing changes which user settings are applied to users logging on to specific computers.

Loopback Processing modifies how User Configuration settings are applied on specific computers (typically kiosks, lab machines, or Terminal Servers). In Replace mode, the user's normal User Configuration GPOs are completely replaced by the User Configuration settings from the GPOs linked to the computer's OU. This means the user gets the user settings defined for the computer's location, not their own OU. In Merge mode (index 3 describes merge behavior), the computer's user settings are merged with the user's own settings, with computer GPO settings winning conflicts. Replace mode is a strict override, not an additive merge.

Default domain password policies (minimum length, complexity, lockout) apply only when configured in a GPO linked at the domain level. GPOs linked to an OU can contain Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies, but these settings affect the local SAM accounts on computers in that OU — not the domain user accounts. To enforce different password policies for subsets of domain users, administrators use Fine-Grained Password Policies (PSOs — Password Settings Objects), which are a separate AD feature introduced in Windows Server 2008, not standard GPO links to OUs.

Group Policy Preferences (GPP) configure settings that are applied as defaults but are not enforced — users can modify them after the preference is applied. For example, a mapped drive or desktop shortcut configured as a preference can be deleted by the user; the preference re-applies it at the next refresh but does not prevent changes. Group Policy Policies (true managed settings) write to protected registry keys or system configuration areas that users cannot change without administrative rights. Preferences are not more secure, not faster, and bandwidth is not a meaningful differentiator between the two.

gpupdate /force triggers an immediate Group Policy refresh on the local computer, re-applying all GPOs regardless of whether they have changed since the last refresh (the /force flag bypasses the change-detection optimization). Without /force, gpupdate only re-applies policies where a version change is detected. gpedit /refresh is not a real command — gpedit.msc is the Local Group Policy Editor GUI, not a command-line tool. gpresult /sync is not a real gpresult parameter (gpresult reports applied GPOs but does not trigger refresh). repadmin /gpo is not a real repadmin flag; repadmin is an AD replication diagnostic tool.

A WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) filter is a query associated with a GPO link. Before applying the GPO, the client evaluates the WMI query against the local system. If the query returns true, the GPO applies; if false, the GPO is skipped. This allows targeting based on system properties — operating system version, installed software, hardware, free disk space, or any WMI-exposed attribute. WMI filters are entirely unrelated to malware blocking, network traffic filtering, or permission management.

When you back up a GPO using the Group Policy Management Console (GPMC) or Backup-GPO PowerShell cmdlet, the backup captures the GPO's settings — security settings, registry-based Administrative Template settings, software installation configuration, scripts, and other policy data. It does NOT capture GPO links. Links are the associations between a GPO and an AD container (site, domain, or OU), and they live in the AD container object, not in the GPO itself. Restoring a backed-up GPO restores the settings but does not re-create any links; links must be manually recreated or managed separately.

HTTP.sys is the kernel-mode driver in Windows that listens on TCP port 80 (and 443 for HTTPS) and handles all incoming HTTP/HTTPS traffic before it reaches any user-mode process. Running in kernel mode, HTTP.sys benefits from performance and security advantages (fewer context switches, isolation from user-mode crashes). It passes accepted requests to W3SVC for routing. W3SVC (World Wide Web Publishing Service) is a user-mode service that manages the lifecycle of worker processes. WAS (Windows Process Activation Service) handles process activation. w3wp.exe is the IIS worker process that runs application pool code.

An application pool is a container that groups one or more web applications and runs them inside a dedicated w3wp.exe worker process. The core benefit is isolation: a crash, memory leak, or security compromise in one application pool does not affect applications in other pools. Additionally, each pool can run under a different identity, enabling least-privilege separation between hosted applications. Application pools do not store content (that lives in the file system), do not handle caching (handled by the kernel cache in HTTP.sys and output cache modules), and do not manage SSL certificates (certificates are bound at the site level).

A host header (also called the HTTP Host: request header) contains the domain name the client is connecting to (e.g., www.example.com). IIS reads the Host header and routes the request to the matching site binding. This allows multiple websites — each with a different hostname — to share the same IP address and port (e.g., all on port 80 or 443). Without host headers, hosting multiple sites would require separate IP addresses or separate ports. The port number and IP address alone cannot differentiate between sites that share them. Protocol (HTTP vs HTTPS) is part of the binding definition but does not by itself enable multi-site on the same address/port combination.

Starting with IIS 7.5 (Windows Server 2008 R2), the default application pool identity is ApplicationPoolIdentity. This is a virtual account automatically created by IIS with a name of the form IIS AppPool\<PoolName>. It has minimal privileges — enough to serve web content and write to the configured log directory — and is significantly more restricted than LocalSystem (which has full machine access) or NetworkService (which can access network resources using the computer account). ApplicationPoolIdentity is the secure default and Microsoft's recommended identity for most application pools.

New-Website is the PowerShell cmdlet from the WebAdministration module used to create a new IIS website. It accepts parameters for site name (-Name), physical path (-PhysicalPath), port (-Port), IP address, and host header. Add-Website is not a real cmdlet in the WebAdministration module (IIS uses New- for creation, following PowerShell verb conventions for object creation). Create-IISSite is not a real cmdlet (Create- is not an approved PowerShell verb). Install-Website does not exist.

The structural distinction between a virtual directory and an application in IIS is that an application is an execution boundary: it has its own application pool assignment and runs as a distinct managed code entry point. A virtual directory is a mapping of a URL path to a file system location, but it shares the application pool and application boundaries of its parent. Multiple virtual directories can exist under one application. Applications support all frameworks that IIS supports (not just .NET). Neither virtual directories nor applications have an inherent speed difference or protocol limitation relative to each other.

Windows Authentication (using Kerberos or NTLM) enables seamless Single Sign-On for domain users: the user's already-established domain credentials (obtained at Windows logon) are transparently passed to IIS without prompting for a username/password. The browser negotiates authentication automatically using Kerberos tickets for intranet sites. Basic Authentication transmits base64-encoded credentials in the clear (requires HTTPS) and always requires a credential prompt. Forms Authentication uses custom HTML login forms and session cookies — not SSO. Digest Authentication sends credentials as an MD5 hash, requires credential prompts, and does not provide the transparent SSO experience that Windows Authentication delivers.

WAS (Windows Process Activation Service) is the IIS component responsible for managing the lifecycle of worker processes (w3wp.exe). It starts worker processes when requests arrive, monitors their health, recycles them on schedule or when they exceed resource thresholds (memory, CPU, request count, elapsed time), and shuts them down during idle timeout. WAS also supports activation protocols beyond HTTP (named pipes, TCP) through the Windows Activation Framework. SSL certificate management is handled at the site-binding level in IIS. HTTP response compression is handled by the Static/Dynamic Compression modules. Access logging is handled by the IIS Logging module.

Self-signed certificates are not issued by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) and therefore generate browser security warnings for all users visiting a site. On a public-facing production site, these warnings destroy user trust, cause browsers to block the connection by default, and fail PCI-DSS, HIPAA, and other compliance requirements. Self-signed certificates are appropriate in development environments, testing scenarios, and internal lab servers where administrators can install the certificate into their trusted root store and where no external users are involved. For production, certificates must come from a publicly trusted CA (commercial CA or a publicly trusted free CA such as Let's Encrypt).

IIS uses an overlapping recycle mechanism: when a recycle is triggered (by schedule, memory limit, request count, or manually), a new w3wp.exe worker process is started and begins accepting new requests while the old worker process continues to serve its in-flight requests until they complete or a timeout expires. This "web garden" handoff minimizes downtime — most users notice no interruption. The old process is then cleanly terminated. The website is not deleted. IIS itself does not restart (only the worker process for that pool restarts). Session state persistence depends on the session storage mechanism: in-process session state (stored in the old worker process's memory) is lost on recycle, but out-of-process session state (SQL Server, Redis, State Service) survives.

The RD Connection Broker is the load-balancing and session-management role service in an RDS deployment. It tracks which users have existing disconnected sessions and reconnects them to the correct RD Session Host rather than starting a new session. It also distributes new connection requests across Session Hosts in a collection to balance load. Without a Connection Broker, users in multi-host deployments would land on random Session Hosts with no reconnection continuity.

In session-based (RDSH) deployments, multiple users share a single Windows Server OS instance running on an RD Session Host; each user gets an isolated session within that shared OS. In VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure), each user gets their own dedicated virtual machine running a client OS (Windows 10/11). VDI delivers a more personalized and isolated experience at the cost of greater infrastructure overhead (one VM per user versus one server per many users).

RD Gateway wraps RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) traffic inside an HTTPS tunnel using the RPC-over-HTTPS or HTTP transport. From the network perimeter, only port 443 needs to be open inbound — the same port used for web traffic. This allows remote users to connect to internal RDS resources through firewalls and proxies that block port 3389, without requiring a separate VPN. The gateway authenticates users and enforces connection authorization policies (CAPs) before allowing RDP sessions through.

RD Gateway uses two complementary policy types. A Connection Authorization Policy (CAP) defines WHO can connect through the gateway — it specifies which user groups are permitted and what authentication methods are required (password, smart card, or both). A Resource Authorization Policy (RAP) defines WHAT those authenticated users can connect to — it specifies which internal computers or computer groups are reachable through the gateway. Both policies must match for a connection to succeed.

Beyond the base Windows Server license, every user or device connecting to an RDS deployment must be covered by an RDS Client Access License (CAL). There are two CAL types: RDS User CALs (per named user, any device) and RDS Device CALs (per device, any user). RDS CALs are managed and issued by an RD Licensing server. An RDS deployment runs in a 120-day grace period without a licensing server, after which connections are refused.

RemoteApp is an RDS feature that publishes individual server-side applications to end users without presenting a full remote desktop. The application runs on an RD Session Host but appears in the user's taskbar and windows just like a locally installed program — it has its own window, integrates with the local desktop, and can receive files dragged from the local system. Users interact with one application, not an entire remote desktop session.

Windows Server 2022 (and 2019/2016) allows RDS to function for 120 days without a configured RD Licensing server. During this grace period, the server issues temporary per-device tokens so that RDP connections succeed. After 120 days, if a valid RD Licensing server with sufficient CALs is not reachable, new connections are refused with a licensing error. This grace period exists to give administrators time to set up licensing infrastructure, not as a permanent bypass.

User Profile Disks are VHD/VHDX files stored on a file share, one per user, that are mounted dynamically when a user session begins on any RD Session Host in a collection. The user's profile data — desktop settings, application preferences, documents stored in redirected folders — travels with the disk regardless of which Session Host the Connection Broker assigns the user to. Without UPDs (or an equivalent like FSLogix), users in multi-host collections would get a blank or inconsistent profile each session depending on which host they land on.

New-RDSessionCollection is the cmdlet from the RemoteDesktop module that creates a session-based collection in an RDS deployment. A session collection defines a group of RD Session Host servers, the users who can connect to them, and collection-level settings (UPD path, client device redirection, etc.). The New- verb follows PowerShell's approved verb conventions for creating new objects.

RD Connection Broker stores session and user-mapping data in a local Windows Internal Database (WID) by default. To achieve high availability (active-active Connection Broker clusters), the WID must be replaced with a dedicated SQL Server instance (or SQL Server Always On Availability Group) that all Connection Broker nodes share. This shared SQL backend is the Microsoft-supported HA configuration; it allows any broker node to handle reconnections for sessions created by any other node.

The Root CA's private key is the single most critical asset in the entire PKI. If the Root CA key is compromised, every certificate ever issued under that root must be revoked and the entire PKI hierarchy must be rebuilt. The industry-standard mitigation is to keep the Root CA offline (powered down) and physically air-gapped, storing it in a secure facility. It is brought online only for the rare operations of signing Subordinate CA certificates or publishing CRLs, then immediately taken offline again. This means a compromise of online infrastructure cannot reach the root key.

Certificate Templates (available on Enterprise CAs integrated with Active Directory) are definitions stored in AD that specify: the certificate's purpose (key usage and extended key usage), validity period, subject name construction (from AD attributes or supplied by requester), cryptographic requirements (key length, provider, hash algorithm), and who is allowed to enroll (security group filtering). When a requester asks for a certificate, they select a template; the CA generates the certificate according to the template's constraints. Templates eliminate per-request manual configuration and enforce policy uniformly.

A Certificate Revocation List (CRL) is a signed, time-stamped file published by the CA on a scheduled cadence (e.g., every 7 days for a base CRL). Clients download the CRL and cache it locally; the list tells them which certificate serial numbers have been revoked. The latency between actual revocation and a client learning about it is bounded by the CRL publication interval. Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) is a request-response protocol: a client sends a certificate's serial number to an OCSP Responder and receives a real-time signed status (good, revoked, or unknown). OCSP provides current-state revocation data without waiting for the next CRL publication cycle.

An Enterprise CA is joined to a domain and integrated with Active Directory. This integration enables: certificate templates (defined in AD), automatic enrollment via Group Policy (computers and users receive certificates without manual interaction), subject information auto-populated from AD attributes, and publication of issued certificates to the AD user or computer object. Standalone CAs lack AD integration — they use a flat request/approval model and cannot use certificate templates or autoenrollment.

Every certificate in the hierarchy — issued by Subordinate CAs, Issuing CAs, and ultimately trusted by clients because the chain leads to the Root — derives its trustworthiness from the Root CA's private key. If that key is compromised, an attacker can issue arbitrary certificates that chain to the trusted root and pass all validation checks. There is no recovery path: the Root CA certificate must be revoked and removed from all trust stores, all Subordinate and Issuing CAs must be retired, all issued certificates are invalidated, and a new PKI hierarchy must be built from a new Root CA. This is why keeping the Root CA offline and air-gapped is non-negotiable.

Key Archival is a CA feature that stores an encrypted copy of the private key associated with an encryption certificate in the CA database at enrollment time. If the user later loses their private key (hardware failure, deleted profile, corrupted keystore), a Key Recovery Agent (KRA) can retrieve the archived key from the CA and restore it to the user. This is critical for certificates used to encrypt data (EFS, encrypted email): without key recovery, data encrypted with a lost private key is permanently inaccessible.

Digital signatures are designed to provide non-repudiation: proof that a specific private key produced the signature, and therefore that its owner signed the document. Non-repudiation is only meaningful if no one else has ever had access to that private key. Key archival gives the CA (and Key Recovery Agents) a copy of the private key, which breaks non-repudiation: the CA or a KRA could theoretically produce signatures using the archived key, undermining the legal and technical basis of the signature. For this reason, signature-only keys must never be archived. Only encryption keys, where data recovery is more important than exclusivity, should have archival enabled.

Root CA certificates have validity periods measured in decades (10-25 years is common). Because the root key must remain cryptographically secure for its entire validity period — and because cryptanalytic capabilities improve over time — a larger key is required for root certificates than for shorter-lived issued certificates. NIST and Microsoft PKI design guidance recommend 4096-bit RSA (or equivalent elliptic curve key strength) for Root CAs. Subordinate CAs and end-entity certificates may use 2048-bit keys for their shorter validity periods, but the root warrants the higher strength.

Autoenrollment is configured through Group Policy. In a GPO linked to the target computers or users, navigate to Computer Configuration (or User Configuration) > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Public Key Policies > Certificate Services Client - Auto-Enrollment. Set the configuration to Enabled and select the options to renew expired certificates, update pending certificates, and remove revoked certificates. When the GPO applies, computers contact the Enterprise CA, request certificates for which they have Enroll permission on applicable templates, and install them automatically — no administrator or user interaction is required per machine.

A complete CA backup requires three components. (1) The CA database (.edb and log files) contains the record of every certificate ever issued, revoked, and pending, plus archived private keys for key recovery. (2) The CA private key (and its certificate) is what makes the CA cryptographically authoritative; without it, a restored CA cannot sign new certificates or CRLs. (3) The CA configuration (registry keys under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration) defines templates, policy modules, extensions, and CRL publication points. certutil -backup or the Certification Authority MMC backup wizard captures all three. Losing any one of these three components means the restored CA either cannot operate or cannot be trusted.

Switch Independent mode does not require any configuration on the physical switch. The switch is unaware that the NICs are teamed; each NIC can connect to a different physical switch, making the team resilient to a complete switch failure. The server-side teaming software handles distribution and failover without relying on switch-side coordination. This makes Switch Independent the right choice when switch configuration access is unavailable or when connecting to switches from different vendors that do not share teaming awareness.

IEEE 802.3ad defines the Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP), which enables multiple physical network links to be dynamically bundled into a single logical link. The 802.3ad standard specifies the LACPDU (Link Aggregation Control Protocol Data Unit) frames exchanged between the host and switch to negotiate which ports participate in the aggregation group. LACP is also referenced as the IEEE 802.1AX-2008 standard in its revised form, though 802.3ad remains the commonly cited identifier in vendor documentation including Microsoft.

The IEEE 802.1Q standard defines a 12-bit VLAN identifier field in the tag, which gives a mathematical range of 0-4095. However, VLAN 0 is reserved (it indicates the frame carries a priority tag but no VLAN membership) and VLAN 4095 is also reserved. VLAN 1 is the default native VLAN on most switches. The usable range for assigning VLANs to switch ports and virtual network adapters is therefore 1 through 4094.

Software Defined Networking (SDN) refers to an architecture that decouples the network control plane (deciding where traffic goes) from the data plane (forwarding traffic). In Windows Server, SDN is implemented via the Network Controller role, which provides a centralized API-driven management point for virtual networks, software load balancers, RAS Gateways, and network policies in Hyper-V environments. SDN enables programmatic, automated network configuration at scale in data center deployments.

New-NetFirewallRule is the cmdlet in the NetSecurity module that creates a new Windows Defender Firewall rule. It accepts parameters for direction (-Direction Inbound/Outbound), action (-Action Allow/Block), protocol (-Protocol TCP/UDP), local port (-LocalPort), program (-Program), display name (-DisplayName), and profile (-Profile Domain/Private/Public). Example: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Allow SQL" -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 1433 -Action Allow.

IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) is a suite of protocols that operates at the IP layer (Layer 3) to provide authentication and encryption of IP packets. In Windows Server, IPsec is configured through Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security via Connection Security Rules. IPsec can authenticate communicating parties (using Kerberos, certificates, or pre-shared keys), encrypt traffic in transit (ESP — Encapsulating Security Payload), and verify packet integrity (AH — Authentication Header). Common uses include server-to-server traffic isolation, domain isolation policies, and protecting management traffic.

DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) value 46 corresponds to the Expedited Forwarding (EF) Per-Hop Behavior defined in RFC 3246. EF is the standard QoS marking for real-time, low-latency, low-jitter traffic — exactly the properties required by VoIP (Voice over IP) and video conferencing. Network devices configured to honor DSCP markings give EF-marked packets priority queuing and guaranteed forwarding, minimizing delay and packet loss. DSCP 46 is the universally recommended marking for VoIP RTP media streams.

Test-NetConnection (from the NetTCPIP module) performs connectivity diagnostics that go beyond basic ICMP ping. With the -Port parameter, it attempts a TCP connection to the specified port and reports whether the port is open (TcpTestSucceeded: True/False), along with RTT, interface used, and DNS resolution. Example: Test-NetConnection -ComputerName server01 -Port 443 — this is the standard tool for verifying that a service port is reachable without needing a third-party tool.

Network Address Translation (NAT) maps private IPv4 addresses (RFC 1918 ranges: 10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x) to one or more public IP addresses when traffic exits to the internet. This allows organizations to use private addressing internally (not globally routable, not ISP-assigned) while sharing a small pool of public addresses. In Windows Server, NAT is implemented through the Routing and Remote Access Service (RRAS) or via the new Windows NAT (WinNAT) for container and Hyper-V networking scenarios. Port Address Translation (PAT) is the most common form, using port numbers to multiplex many private sessions through a single public IP.

In Hyper-V, each virtual machine communicates through a virtual switch port. Hyper-V Port load balancing assigns each virtual switch port to a specific physical NIC team member. This ensures that all traffic from a given VM consistently exits through the same physical NIC, which avoids the out-of-order packet problem that affects TCP performance when flows are split across multiple paths. Because a VM's traffic is always bound to one team member, the switch also sees a consistent MAC address per port, which prevents the MAC-flapping issues that arise with other algorithms in virtualized environments.

An Active Directory site is a collection of IP subnets that represent a well-connected (typically LAN-speed) portion of the network. Sites serve two primary functions. First, they control replication: inter-site replication traffic is compressed, scheduled, and routed through site links, preventing branch-office WAN links from being saturated by continuous AD replication. Second, they direct client authentication: when a computer logs in, the Netlogon service finds a domain controller in the same site (using subnet-to-site mappings), minimizing authentication traffic across WAN links and reducing logon latency.

Within a site, Active Directory uses a change notification model. When a DC writes a change, it waits 15 seconds (the default initial notification delay, to allow for additional changes to batch together), then notifies its replication partners. Partners then pull the changes. With multiple replication partners in a ring topology, intrasite replication propagates changes across all DCs in a site within minutes. The 15-second delay is configurable via registry keys (ReplicationNotifyFirstDsaDelay and ReplicationNotifySubsequentDsaDelay). This near-real-time behavior is why intrasite links do not use scheduled compression.

A site link is an Active Directory object (created in Sites and Services) that represents a network path between two or more sites. It defines three properties that govern how intersite replication flows: cost (lower cost = preferred path), replication interval (how frequently the KCC schedules replication across this link), and schedule (which hours of day replication is permitted). Site links are logical — they model the available network connectivity between sites but do not represent physical cables. The KCC uses site links and their costs to compute the optimal replication topology.

Site link cost is a relative numeric value (default 100) that the KCC uses as a metric when computing the replication topology — analogous to routing metrics in IP routing protocols. A lower cost indicates a more desirable path: the KCC prefers routes with lower total cost when multiple paths exist between sites. Administrators set lower costs on site links representing faster, more reliable, or lower-latency connections (e.g., a 10 Gbps direct fiber link costs 10, while a 1 Mbps MPLS backup link costs 500). This directs the KCC to route replication over the better path while keeping the expensive path for failover only.

The default replication interval on a newly created site link is 180 minutes (3 hours). This means the KCC schedules replication across the site link every 3 hours during the windows defined by the site link schedule. Administrators can reduce this interval (minimum 15 minutes) to increase replication frequency over WAN links at the cost of higher bandwidth consumption, or increase it to reduce bandwidth usage. The default 3-hour interval is a balance point for typical WAN-connected branch offices.

A bridgehead server is the DC within a site that the KCC designates to send and receive intersite replication traffic on behalf of the site. Rather than every DC in a site replicating directly with DCs in remote sites (which would generate excessive WAN traffic), all intersite replication flows through the bridgehead server. The bridgehead pulls changes from its intersite partner and then distributes them to other DCs in its site via normal intrasite replication. The KCC automatically selects a Preferred Bridgehead Server, or administrators can designate one manually via Sites and Services.

When a client's IP address does not match any subnet registered in Sites and Services, Netlogon cannot determine which site the client belongs to. In this case, Netlogon queries DNS for SRV records for _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.<domain> without a site qualifier and selects a responding DC from the returned list, which may be in any site. This can result in a client in a branch office authenticating against a DC in a distant data center across a slow WAN link, causing slow logons. The fix is to register the client's subnet in Sites and Services and map it to the appropriate site.

The Knowledge Consistency Checker is a process that runs on every DC (as part of the NTDS service) and is responsible for automatically calculating and maintaining the AD replication topology. Every 15 minutes, the KCC evaluates the current set of DCs, sites, site links, and site link bridges, then creates or removes Connection objects representing replication partnerships. The KCC ensures that every DC can receive changes from every other DC within a bounded number of hops (no more than 3 hops within a site, and efficient intersite paths via bridgehead servers). If a DC is added, removed, or fails, the KCC automatically adjusts the topology.

repadmin /replsummary queries all domain controllers in the domain and produces a table showing the last replication attempt time, whether it succeeded or failed, and the number of consecutive replication failures for each DC-to-DC partnership. It is the standard first-look tool for identifying replication problems across the domain. Other useful repadmin sub-commands include /showrepl (detailed per-partner status for a specific DC), /replicate (force immediate replication between two DCs), and /syncall (synchronize a DC with all its partners).

A Read-Only Domain Controller (RODC) holds a read-only replica of the AD database. Changes can never be written directly to an RODC — it only receives replication from writable DCs, never sends changes back. This one-way replication model is the key security property of the RODC: even if an RODC is physically compromised (theft in a branch office, for example), an attacker cannot write malicious data to the AD database through it. The RODC pulls only the account data specified by its Password Replication Policy, further limiting the exposure of credential material.
