explanations: The 3-2-1 rule is the foundational backup strategy: maintain 3 copies of data (the production copy plus 2 backups), store those copies on at least 2 different media types (e.g., local disk and tape, or local disk and cloud object storage), and keep at least 1 copy offsite (protecting against site-level disasters such as fire, flood, or theft). Any single failure — a disk crash, a ransomware encryption, a building fire — can only affect a subset of the copies, ensuring at least one clean copy survives. The rule was popularized by photographer Peter Krogh and is now considered the baseline requirement for enterprise backup strategies.

A differential backup captures all data changed since the last full backup. Each successive differential backup grows larger because it always measures from the full baseline. Restore requires the full backup plus only the most recent differential — two sets. An incremental backup captures only data changed since the last backup of any type (full or incremental). Each incremental is small because it measures only since the last backup. Restore requires the full backup plus every incremental in sequence — more sets, more complex restore. The trade-off: differential is faster to restore (fewer sets), incremental is faster to back up (smaller sets).

The System State on a domain controller is a logically consistent snapshot of the components required to restore the DC's role. It includes: the Active Directory database (NTDS.dit and associated log files), which contains the entire AD data store; the SYSVOL folder, which holds Group Policy templates and netlogon scripts replicated to all DCs; the registry (HKLM\SYSTEM and other hives); boot files (boot sector, BCD store, ntoskrnl.exe, hal.dll, and system protected files). The wbadmin start systemstatebackup command captures all of these components as a unit. Backing up only the AD database without SYSVOL and the registry leaves the DC unable to function after restore.

Bare Metal Recovery restores a complete server image (operating system, drivers, roles, configuration, and data) to a machine that has no pre-existing operating system — effectively to blank or replacement hardware. Windows Server Backup supports BMR via the wbadmin start recovery command or through the Windows Recovery Environment. BMR is the appropriate recovery method when the original hardware has failed completely and the server must be rebuilt on a new physical machine or clean virtual machine from a backup image, rather than in-place repair of a partially functional system.

VSS (Volume Shadow Copy Service) coordinates with applications and the file system to produce a point-in-time, consistent snapshot of a volume even while files are open and being written to. Without VSS, a backup of a database or mail store that is actively being modified would capture partially-written pages, resulting in a corrupt backup. VSS works by requesting that VSS-aware writers (SQL Server, Exchange, NTDS, etc.) flush their in-memory data to disk and pause I/O momentarily while a shadow copy is taken. The actual data capture uses a copy-on-write mechanism; once the snapshot exists, normal I/O resumes while the backup reads from the shadow copy.

An authoritative restore stamps restored AD objects with a USN (Update Sequence Number) that is higher than any existing copy of those objects on other DCs. This tells the replication engine that the restored objects are the "authoritative" version and should be replicated to all other DCs, overwriting the deleted state. Without an authoritative restore (a non-authoritative restore), the restored DC would receive the deletion from its replication partners during normal convergence, and the recovered objects would be deleted again. Authoritative restore is the correct procedure when objects were accidentally deleted from AD and AD Recycle Bin either is not enabled or the tombstone lifetime has expired.

RPO defines how much data loss a business can tolerate, expressed as a time period. If the RPO is 4 hours, the business can accept losing up to 4 hours of data in the event of a disaster. RPO drives backup frequency: to meet a 4-hour RPO, backups must run at least every 4 hours. RPO is paired with RTO (Recovery Time Objective), which is the maximum acceptable downtime before the system must be restored. RPO answers "how old can our last good backup be?" — RTO answers "how long can we be down?" Both are defined by business impact analysis, not by technical capability.

New-WBPolicy is from the WindowsServerBackup module and creates an empty Windows Server Backup policy object in memory. After creating the policy object, administrators add configuration using additional cmdlets: Add-WBVolume (add volumes to back up), Add-WBSystemState (include System State), New-WBFileSpec + Add-WBFileSpec (include/exclude specific files), Set-WBSchedule (configure the backup schedule), and Set-WBPolicy (commit the policy to the system). Example workflow: $policy = New-WBPolicy; Add-WBVolume -Policy $policy -Volume C:; Set-WBSchedule -Policy $policy -Schedule 02:00; Set-WBPolicy -Policy $policy.

When AD Recycle Bin is enabled (requires Windows Server 2008 R2 or later forest functional level), deleted AD objects are moved to a logical recycle bin state rather than being immediately tombstoned. During the Deleted Object Lifetime (180 days by default, matching the tombstone lifetime), the deleted object retains all of its original attributes — group memberships, manager links, email addresses, SID history, etc. — and can be restored using Restore-ADObject or the Active Directory Administrative Center with a single step. After the Deleted Object Lifetime expires, the object progresses to the recycled (stripped) state, and eventually tombstone removal. Important: once enabled, AD Recycle Bin cannot be disabled.

A backup that has never been tested is an assumption, not a guarantee. Backup software can report successful completion while the backup file is corrupt, incomplete, or stored on a media type that the restore environment cannot read. The only proof that a backup works is a successful restore — ideally to an isolated test environment using the actual backup file, verifying that critical services come online and that representative data is intact and correct. Organizations that discover their backups are broken during an actual disaster have no recovery option. Regular restore testing (monthly, quarterly, or as required by policy) is the only way to validate the backup chain end to end.

explanations: Windows Firewall uses three network profiles to apply security settings appropriate to the type of network a device is connected to. Per the Microsoft Learn Windows Firewall Overview: "Windows Firewall offers three network profiles: domain, private and public. The network profiles are used to assign rules. For example, you can allow a specific application to communicate on a private network, but not on a public network." Each profile defines an independent set of firewall rules and defaults that activate automatically based on network location awareness.

The default behavior of Windows Firewall for inbound traffic is to block connections unless they are explicitly permitted by a rule or are responses to solicited outbound traffic. Per the Microsoft Learn Windows Firewall Overview: "The default behavior of Windows Firewall is to: block all incoming traffic, unless solicited or matching a rule." This secure-by-default posture means that no unsolicited inbound connection is permitted without an administrator explicitly creating an allow rule. Outbound traffic follows the opposite default: it is allowed unless a rule blocks it.

The Domain network profile is automatically applied based on domain controller reachability. Per the Microsoft Learn Windows Firewall Overview: "The domain network profile is automatically applied to a device that is joined to an Active Directory domain, when it detects the availability of a domain controller." Unlike the Private and Public profiles, the Domain profile cannot be set manually — Windows applies it automatically through Network Location Awareness when it confirms the device is connected to a network that contains a reachable domain controller for the device's domain. This automatic trust assignment allows domain-joined computers to receive a less restrictive set of rules appropriate for the managed corporate network environment.

Connection Security Rules in Windows Firewall with Advanced Security are the mechanism for configuring IPsec policies between two endpoints. They specify when and how traffic between computers is authenticated and optionally encrypted using Internet Protocol security (IPsec). The Microsoft Learn Windows Firewall command-line guide explicitly covers Connection Security Rules under its "Deploy basic IPsec rule settings" section, stating: "An Internet Protocol security (IPsec) policy consists of rules that determine IPsec behavior. IPsec supports network-level peer authentication, data origin authentication, data integrity, data confidentiality (encryption), and replay protection." Connection Security Rules are distinct from standard inbound/outbound firewall rules: where firewall rules allow or block traffic, Connection Security Rules secure traffic using IPsec — defining authentication requirements, cryptographic proposals, and whether connections must be authenticated, encrypted, or both.

New-NetFirewallRule is the PowerShell cmdlet in the NetSecurity module that creates a new firewall rule. Per its description: "Creates a new inbound or outbound firewall rule and adds the rule to the target computer." The cmdlet supports all standard rule parameters including -DisplayName, -Direction (Inbound/Outbound), -Protocol, -LocalPort, -RemotePort, -Action (Allow/Block), and -Profile (Domain/Private/Public). It can create rules on the local computer or target a Group Policy Object via -PolicyStore. Rules created with this cmdlet become effective immediately on the local computer.

HTTPS traffic arrives at a server as inbound traffic on TCP port 443. To permit external clients to connect to a service (such as a web server or an application that uses HTTPS), the administrator creates an inbound rule targeting TCP port 443. The Microsoft Learn "Configure Firewall Rules With Group Policy" guide documents the procedure for creating inbound port rules: "This type of rule allows any program that listens on a specified TCP or UDP port to receive network traffic sent to that port." HTTPS uses TCP as its transport protocol (not UDP), and the traffic flows inbound to the server receiving client connections. The rule must therefore be directional (Inbound), protocol-specific (TCP), and port-specific (443).

The Public profile is the most restrictive of the three Windows Firewall profiles because it is designed for use on networks where other connected devices and the network infrastructure itself cannot be trusted. Per the Microsoft Learn Windows Firewall Overview: "The public network profile is designed with higher security in mind for public networks, like Wi-Fi hotspots, coffee shops, airports, hotels, etc. It's the default profile for unidentified networks." Because public networks may be shared with unknown or potentially hostile parties — and because there is no domain controller or other trust anchor to authenticate the environment — Windows applies stricter inbound rules under the Public profile to minimize the device's exposure.

The "Log dropped packets" setting instructs Windows Firewall to write a record to the firewall log file each time it drops an inbound packet. Per the Microsoft Learn Windows Firewall logging guide: "To create a log entry when Windows Defender Firewall drops an incoming network packet, change Log dropped packets to Yes." The log file records the time, protocol, source and destination addresses, and port for each dropped packet. The default log path is %windir%\system32\logfiles\firewall\pfirewall.log. This setting is essential for troubleshooting blocked connections and for security monitoring — it provides a record of traffic that was rejected, which can reveal scanning attempts or misconfigured clients.

RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol, TCP 3389) and SMB (Server Message Block, TCP 445) are internal management and file-sharing protocols that are routinely exploited when exposed to the internet. Microsoft's Azure network security best practices guide explicitly addresses RDP under the heading "Disable RDP/SSH Access to virtual machines": "We recommend that you disable direct RDP and SSH access to your Azure virtual machines from the internet." The same guidance describes brute-force attacks as the primary threat: "attackers can use brute force techniques to gain access to Azure virtual machines." SMB port 445 has a well-documented history of critical internet-facing vulnerabilities. Both protocols are designed for use within trusted network boundaries, not for direct internet exposure. The recommended alternative for remote management is VPN, Azure Bastion, or Just-In-Time access — not direct port exposure.

Test-NetConnection is the PowerShell cmdlet in the NetTCPIP module that performs diagnostic connectivity tests including TCP port reachability. Per its description: "The Test-NetConnection cmdlet displays diagnostic information for a connection. It supports ping test, TCP test, route tracing, and route selection diagnostics." Using the -Port parameter, it attempts a TCP connection to the specified port and returns TcpTestSucceeded : True or False in its output. For example, Test-NetConnection -ComputerName server01 -Port 443 tests whether TCP port 443 is reachable on the target, which directly reveals whether a firewall rule is permitting or blocking the connection. This makes it the primary PowerShell tool for verifying firewall rule effectiveness without needing a full client application.

The param() block is the standard, recommended mechanism for declaring named parameters in PowerShell functions and scripts. Per the Microsoft Learn documentation on advanced function parameters: "Parameters are variables declared in the param() statement of a function or scriptblock." The param() block integrates with PowerShell's parameter-binding engine, enabling named parameters, type constraints, mandatory flags, validation attributes, positional binding, and pipeline input — none of which are available when reading from the $args array directly. This is the approach used in advanced functions (functions with [CmdletBinding()]) and in all well-formed scripts.

Per the Microsoft Learn preference variables documentation: "$ErrorActionPreference — Determines how PowerShell responds to a non-terminating error, an error that doesn't stop the cmdlet processing." The variable accepts ActionPreference enumeration values including Continue (the default — display the error and keep running), Stop (halt execution), SilentlyContinue (suppress the error message), and Inquire (prompt the user). It is the canonical preference variable for controlling error-handling behavior across a script or session and can be overridden per-command using the -ErrorAction common parameter.

Register-ScheduledTask is the cmdlet that both defines and registers a scheduled task with the Windows Task Scheduler service on a local computer. Its description states: "Registers a scheduled task definition on a local computer." Registration is the step that makes the task visible to the Task Scheduler service and causes it to run on its defined trigger. Without registration, a task definition is only an in-memory object and will never execute.

DSC stands for Desired State Configuration. The Microsoft Learn overview states: "Microsoft's Desired State Configuration (DSC) is a declarative configuration platform." DSC allows administrators to describe the intended (desired) state of a system in a configuration document, and then enforce or verify that state. The "desired state" naming reflects the core declarative model: you specify what the system should look like, not a sequence of imperative commands to get there.

Start-DscConfiguration is the cmdlet that applies a compiled DSC configuration to one or more target nodes. Per its description: "The Start-DscConfiguration cmdlet applies configuration to nodes." It reads the compiled MOF file from the specified path and pushes configuration settings to the target computers identified by computer name or CIM session. The cmdlet runs as a background job by default and supports -Wait to run synchronously and -Verbose to display progress.

Invoke-Command is the primary PowerShell cmdlet for running commands on local or remote computers. Its description states: "The Invoke-Command cmdlet runs commands on a local or remote computer and returns all output from the commands, including errors. Using a single Invoke-Command command, you can run commands on multiple computers." Remote execution requires PowerShell Remoting (WinRM) to be enabled on the target. Invoke-Command can target one or more computers by name via -ComputerName, or use pre-established CIM or PSSession objects, making it the workhorse of PowerShell-based remote management.

The -ThrottleLimit parameter of Invoke-Command controls how many simultaneous remote connections the cmdlet will establish. Per the documentation: "Specifies the maximum number of concurrent connections that can be established to run this command. If you omit this parameter or enter a value of 0, the default value, 32, is used. The throttle limit applies only to the current command, not to the session or to the computer." This parameter is critical in large-scale environments where running Invoke-Command against hundreds of servers simultaneously could saturate the network.

When you call (execute) a DSC configuration function, it compiles into a MOF document. Per the Microsoft Learn DSC configurations documentation: "Before you can use a DSC Configuration, you have to compile it into a MOF document." When compilation runs, it "Creates a file named localhost.mof in the new directory." The document also notes: "The MOF file contains all the configuration information for the system. Because of this, it's important to keep it secure."

Test-DscConfiguration is the cmdlet that checks whether the actual current configuration of a node matches the desired state defined in its DSC configuration. Per its description: "The Test-DscConfiguration cmdlet tests whether the actual configuration on the nodes matches the desired configuration." If the desired and actual configurations match, the cmdlet returns True; otherwise it returns False. It can target the local computer (default) or remote computers specified by name or CIM session. This cmdlet is essential for drift detection — identifying nodes whose configuration has diverged from the desired state without making any changes.

The #Requires statement is a script-level directive that declares prerequisites for running the script and halts execution immediately if they are not met. Per the Microsoft Learn documentation: "#Requires — Prevents a script from running without the required elements." The long description elaborates: "The #Requires statement prevents a script from running unless the PowerShell version, modules (and version), and edition prerequisites are met. If the prerequisites aren't met, PowerShell doesn't run the script." The supported prerequisites include minimum PowerShell version (-Version), required modules (-Modules), PowerShell edition (-PSEdition), and elevated rights (-RunAsAdministrator). The early-fail behavior is deliberate: it surfaces unmet requirements at parse time rather than midway through a script, preventing partial execution.

The standard IT troubleshooting methodology — as codified by CompTIA — begins with "Identify the problem." Identify the problem is the first step. Before any research, testing, or fix can occur, the technician must gather information: question the user, identify symptoms, and determine what changed. Without a clearly identified problem, every subsequent step risks solving the wrong issue. Identifying the problem includes gathering information, questioning users, identifying symptoms, determining if anything has changed, and duplicating the problem if possible.

dcdiag.exe (Domain Controller Diagnostics) is the Microsoft-supplied command-line tool for testing domain controller health. It runs a battery of tests — including connectivity, replication, services, advertising, and KCC topology checks — and reports PASS/FAIL per test. dcdiag ships as part of the Remote Server Administration Tools (RSAT) and is available directly on domain controllers. A basic invocation is dcdiag (runs all default tests) or dcdiag /test:<TestName> for a specific test.

repadmin (Replication Diagnostics Tool) is the authoritative command-line tool for Active Directory replication administration. The /replsummary subcommand produces a per-partner summary of replication health for all domain controllers in the forest, including the largest delta and failure counts. It is the standard first command an AD administrator runs when investigating replication lag or failures. repadmin ships on all domain controllers and is also available via RSAT. Other useful repadmin subcommands include /showrepl (per-NC detail), /replicate (force immediate replication), and /syncall (full forest synchronization).

Test-NetConnection (from the NetTCPIP module) performs both ICMP reachability testing and TCP port connectivity testing in a single cmdlet. Using the -Port parameter, it attempts a TCP connection to the specified port and returns TcpTestSucceeded : True/False alongside standard ping results. Example: Test-NetConnection -ComputerName dc01.contoso.com -Port 389. This makes it far more useful for troubleshooting specific services (LDAP, RDP, SMB, etc.) than a plain ping.

bootrec.exe is the Windows Recovery Environment command-line tool for repairing boot configuration data. The /fixboot parameter writes a new boot sector to the system partition, replacing a corrupted or missing one. It is run from the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) command prompt — typically accessed by booting from Windows installation media and selecting "Repair your computer." The full suite of bootrec subcommands covers the full boot repair workflow: /fixmbr (repair MBR), /fixboot (repair boot sector), /scanos (scan for Windows installations), and /rebuildbcd (rebuild the Boot Configuration Data store).

In a normal (non-authoritative) restore, the restored DC's objects will be overwritten by the surviving DCs after the restore — effectively pulling in the deleted or corrupted state again. An authoritative restore uses ntdsutil.exe after the non-authoritative restore to mark specific objects as authoritative, which changes their version number so that it is higher than the existing version of the (tombstoned) object. When AD replication runs, the higher version number causes the restored objects to replicate outward TO all other domain controllers, updating the tombstone back to the restored object across the forest. This is the correct technique for recovering accidentally deleted OUs, users, or objects.

sfc.exe (System File Checker) is the Windows command-line utility that scans the integrity of all protected Windows system files and replaces incorrect versions with correct cached copies. The /scannow parameter scans the integrity of all protected system files and repairs files with problems when possible, in a single command. It must be run by a member of the Administrators group (from an elevated command prompt).

Storage Migration Service (SMS) is a Windows Server feature introduced in Windows Server 2019 that orchestrates the end-to-end migration of file servers as a three-step process: inventory the source servers and their files and configuration; transfer (copy) the files, file shares, and security configuration; and optionally cut over to the new servers, where the destination "assume[s] the source servers' former identities so that apps and users don't have to change anything" to access their data. SMS handles Windows Server-to-Windows Server migrations and can also inventory and transfer from Samba/Linux and NetApp CIFS sources. The orchestrator runs on a Windows Server 2019 or later host; the source server can be Windows Server 2003 or later. It is managed from the Windows Admin Center user interface.

Event ID 4771 ("Kerberos pre-authentication failed") is logged on the domain controller's Security event log when a Kerberos client attempts pre-authentication and the KDC rejects it — typically because of a bad password or an expired account. This is the Kerberos-specific authentication failure event and is distinct from NTLM-based failures. Security monitoring tools map 4771 to brute-force and credential-stuffing detection against Kerberos (common against AD). Failure code 0x18 in the event means the wrong password was provided; 0x12 means the client's credentials have been revoked; 0x25 means clock skew too great.

Microsoft's recommended way to upgrade a domain is to do a clean OS install to promote a NEW server to a domain controller running the newer Windows Server version, transfer the operations master (FSMO) roles to it using Move-ADDirectoryServerOperationMasterRole, and then demote and remove the old domain controller. In other words, you introduce an additional (new/intermediary) server into the environment during the transition rather than upgrading the existing server in place — the new server carries the roles and data forward while the old one is retired. Microsoft explicitly states this clean-install-then-promote approach is preferable to an in-place upgrade of an existing DC because it delivers the full Active Directory performance improvements of the new version. "Swing migration" is the common industry term for this introduce-a-new-server-then-cut-over pattern.
